Graphics gallery

Source: vignettes/articles/graphics-gallery.Rmd
graphics-gallery.Rmd

autoplot() and the plot_*() functions return ggplot objects. The figures are ready for a manuscript as they are, and anything about them can be changed with the usual ggplot2 grammar: add labels, scales, themes or layers with +. This gallery shows each figure once, then the changes most often needed before a figure goes into a paper or onto a slide.

The examples use three fits: tuberculosis mortality with empirical quantile intervals (the default), all six causes of death in us_mortality, and the prevalence of each body mass index category in ontario_bmi.

library(joinpoint)
library(ggplot2)

tb <- subset(us_mortality, cause == "Tuberculosis")
fit_tb <- joinpoint(tb, year, rate, kmax = 3)

fit_all <- joinpoint(us_mortality, year, rate, by = "cause", kmax = 3,
                     ci_method = "parametric",
                     control = jp_control(aapc_last = 10))

fit_bmi <- joinpoint(ontario_bmi, year, count = count, population = births,
                     by = "category", type = "percent", kmax = 2,
                     method = "bic", ci_method = "parametric")

Trend figures

autoplot() draws the observed values, the fitted model, the joinpoints and the APC of each segment. plot() prints the same figure and returns the fit, so use autoplot() to modify a figure.

The default figure

The labels sit next to their segments and avoid each other and the fitted curves. An asterisk marks an APC that differs significantly from zero. The shaded band is the pointwise 95% interval of the fitted curve; it is drawn when the fit has empirical quantile intervals.

autoplot(fit_tb)

Uncertainty on the figure

labels = "ci" writes the confidence interval under each APC, and joinpoint_ci = TRUE shades the confidence interval of each joinpoint location. Where a two-line label cannot be placed without overlapping another label or a curve, it may be cut to the APC alone.

autoplot(fit_tb, labels = "ci", joinpoint_ci = TRUE)

Trend direction and a logarithmic axis

color_by = "trend" colors each segment by its direction: significantly increasing, significantly decreasing or stable. On a logarithmic axis (log_y = TRUE) equal percent changes have equal slopes, which suits log-linear models. Several cohorts are drawn as panels, each with its own scale; ncol sets the number of columns.

autoplot(fit_all, color_by = "trend", log_y = TRUE, ncol = 3)

Several series in one panel

layout = "overlay" draws the cohorts in one panel, and cohorts picks some of them by position. With aapc = TRUE each legend entry carries the average annual percent change of the first AAPC range, the full range by default. Segment labels are off by default when series are overlaid, to keep the panel readable.

levels(us_mortality$cause)
#> [1] "Accidents"               "Cancer"                 
#> [3] "Heart Disease"           "Influenza and Pneumonia"
#> [5] "Stroke"                  "Tuberculosis"
autoplot(fit_all, layout = "overlay", cohorts = c(2, 3, 5), aapc = TRUE,
         log_y = TRUE)

Observed values with confidence intervals

When the data carry standard errors, given with se or calculated from count and population, error_bars = TRUE adds the 95% interval of each observed value.

autoplot(fit_bmi, error_bars = TRUE, ncol = 3) +
  labs(x = "Fiscal year (start)", y = "Prevalence (%)")

A model other than the selected one

model draws the best fitting model with a given number of joinpoints instead of the selected one, for example to show a reviewer the simpler alternative.

autoplot(fit_tb, model = 1)

Trend summaries

APCs over time

plot_apc() draws the APC of every segment as a step over the years it covers, with its confidence interval as a band and a reference line at zero. It answers “how fast, and when” more directly than the data.

plot_apc(fit_all, ncol = 3)

AAPC forest plot

plot_aapc() compares average annual percent changes across cohorts and ranges. The fit requested the last ten years in addition to the full range through jp_control(aapc_last = 10); custom ranges are set with aapc_ranges.

plot_aapc(fit_all)

Model selection and diagnostics

All candidate models

plot_models() shows the best fit for every number of joinpoints of one cohort, with the selection statistic of each in its panel title and the selected model highlighted. overlay = TRUE draws them in one panel.

plot_models(fit_tb, ncol = 2)

plot_models(fit_tb, overlay = TRUE)

Selection criteria

plot_selection() draws the selection statistic against the number of joinpoints. For the permutation test it draws the sequence of tests instead; vignette("model-selection") has an example.

plot_selection(fit_tb)

Residuals

plot_residuals() shows the standardized residuals of the selected model against time, as a normal quantile plot, or as an autocorrelation function. vignette("uncertainty") discusses what to do when neighboring residuals are correlated.

plot_residuals(fit_tb)

plot_residuals(fit_tb, type = "qq")

plot_residuals(fit_tb, type = "acf")

Comparing groups

autoplot() of a jp_compare() result draws the separately fitted models (solid) and the model fitted under the null hypothesis (dashed), one panel per pair. vignette("comparing-groups") explains the tests.

pair <- joinpoint(subset(us_mortality, cause %in% c("Stroke", "Heart Disease")),
                  year, rate, by = "cause", kmax = 2, ci_method = "parametric")
autoplot(jp_compare(pair, n_perm = 99), log_y = TRUE)

Customizing the figures

Titles, axis labels and captions

labs() replaces the automatic labels and adds a title and subtitle. A caption given here replaces the automatic note that explains the labels, band and error bars. expression() writes units with superscripts, as in y = expression("Mean BMI (kg/m"^2 * ")").

autoplot(fit_tb) +
  labs(title = "Tuberculosis mortality fell throughout the century",
       subtitle = "The decline was steepest from 1947, when streptomycin came into use",
       x = NULL, y = "Deaths per 100,000 (age adjusted)",
       caption = "Source: CDC National Vital Statistics System, HIST293.")

Axes

The x axis is free to change. Breaks every twenty years, for example:

autoplot(fit_tb) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1900, 2000, by = 20))

autoplot() sets the y scale itself, with room around the curves for the segment labels, and ggplot2 notes when that scale is replaced. To change the y axis, keep the room by passing the expansion autoplot() uses: mult = 0.12 with APC labels (the default), 0.2 with labels = "ci" and 0.05 without labels.

autoplot(fit_bmi, cohorts = 6) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(v) paste0(v, "%"),
                     expand = expansion(mult = 0.12)) +
  labs(x = "Fiscal year (start)", y = "Prevalence")

Text size and fonts

theme_joinpoint() is the theme of every figure. Add it again with a larger base_size for slides or a smaller one for a narrow journal column, and set base_family to a font installed on your system.

autoplot(fit_tb) + theme_joinpoint(base_size = 16)

Any complete ggplot2 theme works too, followed by theme() for details:

autoplot(fit_tb) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title.position = "plot")

Colors

The qualitative palette of scale_color_joinpoint() has eight colors, ordered so that neighboring colors stay distinguishable under the common forms of color vision deficiency. Use it in any ggplot2 figure, together with theme_joinpoint(), to give your own figures the same look:

ggplot(us_mortality, aes(year, rate, color = cause)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_color_joinpoint(name = NULL) +
  theme_joinpoint() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Deaths per 100,000")

To use other colors in a figure colored by cohort, replace the scale for both the color and the fill aesthetics, since the fitted bands are filled in the color of their cohort:

autoplot(fit_all, layout = "overlay", cohorts = c(2, 3, 5), log_y = TRUE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#0B2540", "#2A78D6", "#7F8FA6"),
                     aesthetics = c("colour", "fill"), name = NULL)

Figures built from the result tables

Every result is also a data frame, so any figure can be drawn from scratch. as.data.frame() returns the observed and modeled values with the segment and APC of each point, joinpoints() the joinpoint locations with their intervals, and apc() the segment estimates. Here, the periods between joinpoints are shaded and annotated with their APCs. The shaded rectangles reach beyond the data and coord_cartesian() crops them to the panel, which works on a logarithmic axis too:

pts <- as.data.frame(fit_tb)
seg <- apc(fit_tb)
seg$label <- sprintf("%.1f%%", seg$estimate)
lim <- range(pts$observed, pts$modeled)

ggplot(pts, aes(x)) +
  geom_rect(data = seg, aes(xmin = start, xmax = end, ymin = lim[1] / 10,
                            ymax = lim[2] * 10, fill = factor(segment %% 2)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.25, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(aes(y = observed), color = "#7F8FA6", size = 1.2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = modeled), color = "#2A78D6", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(data = seg, aes(x = (start + end) / 2, y = Inf, label = label),
            vjust = 1.5, size = 3.5, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("white", "#DCE8F7")) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = lim) +
  theme_joinpoint() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Deaths per 100,000")

Saving figures

ggsave() writes a figure at the size it will be printed. Journals usually ask for widths of about 85 mm (one column) or 175 mm (two columns), at least 300 dpi for raster images, or a vector format such as PDF. Choose the size first and set base_size to fit it, rather than scaling a large figure down, so the text ends up at the intended size.

p <- autoplot(fit_tb) + theme_joinpoint(base_size = 9)
ggsave("tuberculosis.pdf", p, width = 85, height = 60, units = "mm")
ggsave("tuberculosis.png", p, width = 85, height = 60, units = "mm",
       dpi = 600, bg = "white")

Add alternative text to figures that are published online. In R Markdown and Quarto documents, the fig.alt chunk option sets it, as on this page.
